# Agent Keyring

> Passwords for the Agentic OS, part of the OpenTrawl suite (https://github.com/opentrawl). Agent Keyring lets Claude Code, Codex or any AI agent sign in to websites with the passwords the user keeps in Apple Passwords. The user approves each password on their Mac (Touch ID), iPhone (Face ID) or Apple Watch (one tap). Free and open source (MIT). No cloud vault, no account and no Tailscale needed.

- Status: the signed and notarised Mac app is available on GitHub Releases today and works straight away with Touch ID. Version 1.1 needs no Tailscale, keeps the user's Macs and iPhones in step through their own iCloud, and lets the iPhone work on its own, with no Mac. The iPhone and Apple Watch apps are in public beta on TestFlight at https://testflight.apple.com/join/W5xBNeMw, or build them from source.
- Made by: Josh Palmer (https://x.com/jjpcodes)
- Licence: MIT
- Source code: https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring
- Releases: https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest
- Website: https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/ (also reachable at https://agent-keyring.jjpcodes.com/)
- Privacy policy: https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/privacy/
- Needs: a Mac on macOS 26 or later with Touch ID (a Mac without Touch ID can opt in to approving with its Mac password), or an iPhone on its own. Optional: an Apple Watch, and other Macs or Linux computers. No Tailscale or other network setup needed.

## Two installs (read this before installing anything)

- **The app** (`Agent Keyring.app`, and the iPhone and Apple Watch app): for the user's own Mac, iPhone and Apple Watch. It holds their passwords, encrypted to each device's Secure Enclave, and asks them to approve or deny each request.
- **The command** (`agent-keyring`): for computers agents run on, such as a headless Mac mini or Mac Studio, a Linux server or a cloud VM. It asks for one password per task, holds no password vault, and joins with `agent-keyring enrol`.

Never install the app on a computer that agents control. If you are running on such a computer, install only the command (see "Agent computers" below). The app on the user's own Mac already includes the command for agents there.

A Mac without Touch ID (a Mac mini or Mac Studio) that is the user's own personal Mac can still run the app: on first launch it asks "How do you use this Mac?", and the user can opt in to approving with their Mac password. Their passwords stay locked to that Mac's Secure Enclave, and no agent can open an Ask password without macOS asking for the Mac password, but a typed password is weaker than Touch ID or Face ID: an agent or tool that knows the Mac login password (for example from a `sudo` prompt) could approve its own requests. Let the user make this choice themselves.

The Mac and iPhone find each other through the user's own iCloud Keychain, end-to-end encrypted by Apple, and keep each other up to date through the user's own iCloud private database. Every Mac and iPhone is an equal: the user can export from Apple Passwords on any of them and the lists merge. There is no account with us.

## Agent install playbook (read this first when asked to install or set up Agent Keyring)

Follow these steps in order. **Cardinal rule:** always explain what you plan to do and ask the user for confirmation before downloading files, probing SSH hosts, installing browser extensions, or changing any files or settings.

### Step 1: Propose the plan and ask first
First ask what the computer you are running on is for. If agents run on it and it is not the Mac where the user keeps and approves their passwords, follow "Agent computers" below instead of these steps.

Tell the user you can:
1. Download the latest signed and notarised Mac release of Agent Keyring from GitHub Releases, verify its SHA-256 checksum, install `/Applications/Agent Keyring.app`, and launch it.
2. Guide them through exporting their passwords from Apple Passwords (`File > Export All Items to App... > Agent Keyring`). Nothing is deleted from Apple Passwords, and every password starts on Ask.
3. Add the Agent Keyring setup line to their agent instructions (`AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`) if they want.
4. Optionally help set up the Chrome-family browser extension, enrol other Macs or Linux servers, or connect an iPhone and Apple Watch.

Ask which parts they want to do before running any download or file edit.

### Step 2: Download, verify, install and launch the Mac app
Once the user agrees, run the script below. It stops at the first step that fails: nothing is unpacked, installed or opened unless the checksum matches. It works in a temporary folder that it deletes after, and stops if the app is already installed (ask the user before replacing it).

```sh
(
  app="/Applications/Agent Keyring.app"
  [ ! -e "$app" ] || { echo "$app is already installed. Ask the user before replacing it." >&2; exit 1; }
  release_json=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest) || exit 1
  # The Mac app zip (Agent-Keyring-VERSION.zip) and SHA256SUMS.txt from the latest release.
  zip_url=$(printf '%s' "$release_json" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; assets=json.load(sys.stdin)["assets"]; print(next(a["browser_download_url"] for a in assets if a["name"].startswith("Agent-Keyring-") and a["name"].endswith(".zip")))') || exit 1
  sums_url=$(printf '%s' "$release_json" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; assets=json.load(sys.stdin)["assets"]; print(next(a["browser_download_url"] for a in assets if a["name"] == "SHA256SUMS.txt"))') || exit 1
  zip_name=$(basename "$zip_url")
  d="$(mktemp -d)" && trap 'rm -r "$d"' EXIT && cd "$d" &&
    curl -fsSL -o "$zip_name" "$zip_url" && curl -fsSL -o SHA256SUMS.txt "$sums_url" &&
    grep "  $zip_name\$" SHA256SUMS.txt | shasum -a 256 -c &&
    ditto -x -k "$zip_name" unpacked &&
    mv "unpacked/Agent Keyring.app" "$app" &&
    open "$app"
)
```

### Step 3: Guide the user through Touch ID and Apple Passwords export
Ask the user to complete the two human-only steps on their Mac:
1. Follow the first-run screen in Agent Keyring (including the practice Touch ID prompt). On a Mac without Touch ID, the app first asks how the Mac is used; the user chooses.
2. Open Apple Passwords, choose `File > Export All Items to App...`, and select **Agent Keyring**. Reassure them nothing is deleted from Apple Passwords and every password starts on **Ask**.

### Step 4: Read the bundled skill and propose optional extras
Once `/Applications/Agent Keyring.app` is installed, run:

```sh
"/Applications/Agent Keyring.app/Contents/Helpers/agent-keyring" skill
```

Follow the bundled skill's instructions. Before probing SSH hosts or modifying any files, tell the user what you suggest setting up next and ask for confirmation:
- **Chrome-family browser extension** (Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Edge, Mac Arc): run `agent-keyring install --browser-profile DIRECTORY` and guide the user to Load unpacked `/Applications/Agent Keyring.app/Contents/Resources/AgentTools/BrowserExtension`.
- **Other Macs or Linux servers:** download the standalone release binary directly from `https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest` (`agent-keyring-linux-amd64`, `agent-keyring-linux-arm64`, or `agent-keyring-darwin-universal`; verify against `SHA256SUMS.txt`, no Nix or Go toolchain required), install to `~/.local/bin/agent-keyring` (the script under "Agent computers" below does this), and enrol with `~/.local/bin/agent-keyring enrol --name "Linux server" --code 'CODE'`, with the one-time code the user's Mac or iPhone shows under **Devices > Add Another Computer…** (no Tailscale needed).
- **iPhone and Apple Watch approval (optional):** install the iPhone app from the TestFlight beta at https://testflight.apple.com/join/W5xBNeMw (or build the iOS and watchOS apps from source). Open the iPhone app, tap Connect, and approve on the Mac. The iPhone finds the Mac through the user's own iCloud Keychain, so both devices need the same Apple Account with iCloud Keychain and iCloud on; Tailscale is not needed. Add Apple Watch from the iPhone app.
- **iPhone only, no Mac:** in the iPhone app, tap **Set Up on This iPhone**, turn Agent Keyring on in Passwords, then in Apple Passwords tap **Export Data to Another App** and choose Agent Keyring. Add Apple Watch and agent computers from the iPhone's Devices tab.

### Agent computers: install the command only
On a computer agents run on (a headless Mac mini or Mac Studio, a Linux server, a cloud VM), install only the standalone command, never the Mac app. Ask the user first, then run the script below. It picks the build for this system, checks it against the release's `SHA256SUMS.txt` before installing it, works in a temporary folder that it deletes after, and leaves your current folder as it was:

```sh
(
  case "$(uname -s)/$(uname -m)" in
    Darwin/*) asset=agent-keyring-darwin-universal ;;
    Linux/x86_64) asset=agent-keyring-linux-amd64 ;;
    Linux/aarch64 | Linux/arm64) asset=agent-keyring-linux-arm64 ;;
    *) echo "No agent-keyring build for $(uname -s) $(uname -m)." >&2; exit 1 ;;
  esac
  verify() { if command -v shasum >/dev/null; then shasum -a 256 -c; else sha256sum -c; fi; }
  base=https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest/download
  d="$(mktemp -d)" && trap 'rm -r "$d"' EXIT && cd "$d" &&
    curl -fsSLO "$base/$asset" && curl -fsSLO "$base/SHA256SUMS.txt" &&
    grep "  $asset\$" SHA256SUMS.txt | verify &&
    mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && install -m 755 "$asset" ~/.local/bin/agent-keyring &&
    echo "Installed ~/.local/bin/agent-keyring"
)
```

Then ask the user to open Agent Keyring on their Mac or iPhone, choose **Devices > Add Another Computer…**, and give you the one-time code (26 characters, or the whole command it shows). Run `~/.local/bin/agent-keyring enrol --name "Mac mini" --code 'CODE'` and tell the user to approve the request on the device that showed the code. The code works once, for 10 minutes; no Tailscale needed.

## What it does

An agent that needs to sign in runs the `agent-keyring` command and asks for one password by website. The user sees the website, the account, which agent on which computer is asking, and the agent's reason. They approve, deny, or deny with a typed or spoken reply that tells the agent what to do instead.

One approval covers one password for one task. It includes retries and the two-factor step, and ends when the agent releases it, when the computer receives Stop, or 30 minutes after approval, whichever comes first. A request nobody answers ends after 10 minutes.

Each password has a rule:

- Ask (every password starts here): the user approves each time.
- Automatic: agents on the computers the user chose get it without asking.
- Blocked: once a computer receives the rule, it refuses new requests.

## How an agent signs in

`agent-keyring skill` prints the full instructions and `agent-keyring --help` lists every command. On the Mac the command is at `"/Applications/Agent Keyring.app/Contents/Helpers/agent-keyring"`; the app doesn't put it on the path. A sign-in looks like this:

```sh
agent-keyring find example.com          # passwords for a website, with their IDs; no secrets
lease=$(agent-keyring lease LOGIN_ID --task "$task" --reason "What the user asked for" --agent "Claude Code")
agent-keyring tabs                      # browser tabs that have the extension
agent-keyring fields --tab "$tab"       # visible fields and their selectors, never values
agent-keyring fill "$lease" --tab "$tab" \
  --username '#username' --password '#password' --submit 'button[type=submit]'
agent-keyring release "$lease"
```

- `lease` waits for the user's answer, for up to 10 minutes, and prints an ID to use for the rest of the task.
- `fill` (Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Edge, and Mac Arc when the browser extension is connected): the agent uses this automatically when available. The extension checks that the page is the website the password was saved for, types into the fields the agent named, submits and clears them so the password stays out of chat and logs. A two-factor step is another `fill` with `--code`.
- `read` (fallback anywhere the extension doesn't run: built-in agent browsers such as Codex, Claude and T3 Code, Safari, desktop apps via computer use, or CLI tools such as `gh`): the agent uses `agent-keyring read "$lease" --field password` (or `--field one-time-code`) straight into the code, app or tool without printing it to output. For example, for a GitHub personal access token saved in the password field: `agent-keyring read "$lease" --field password | gh auth login --with-token`. `read` refuses to print straight to a terminal.
- If the user denies, their reply is printed word for word. Do what it says.
- Never ask the user to type or paste a password that is saved in Agent Keyring.
- The test password is example.com, account you@example.com. Use it to try Agent Keyring out.

## How it is built

- No account and no vault of ours. Your passwords stay encrypted on your own Mac and iPhone with keys kept in their Secure Enclave.
- The user's Macs and iPhones are equal peers and keep each other up to date through the user's own iCloud private database. Every password is sealed (HPKE) to the receiving device's Secure Enclave key before it leaves the device that exported it, so we can't read it, Apple can't, and the user's internet provider can't. The signed lists of devices, passwords and rules are checked by every device. Site and account names are in CloudKit's encrypted fields, end-to-end encrypted when Advanced Data Protection is on. Rule changes merge by last write; Blocked deletes the password everywhere.
- Agents on the Mac ask the Mac app directly. When an agent on another computer needs your iPhone or Apple Watch, it sends an end-to-end encrypted push payload through our stateless blind push relay at `https://push.opentrawl.sh` (AWS `eu-west-1`), which signs it with our Apple Developer push key and forwards it to Apple's push servers without storing raw tokens, IP addresses or payload contents. Self-builders with their own Apple Developer account can run their own relay or push directly to Apple.
- Zero-data-retention encrypted relay at `https://push.opentrawl.sh` (AWS `eu-west-1`, self-hostable via `agent-keyring-box` behind HTTPS with a certificate the iPhone and Apple Watch trust, such as Let's Encrypt): the relay Lambda has zero `console.*` calls, its IAM role has no CloudWatch Logs permissions, and the `/aws/lambda/opentrawl-push-relay` CloudWatch log group is destroyed. Clients hit fixed endpoints (`/v1/box`, `/v1/push`) with random box IDs and access tokens sent only in headers (`x-akr-box`, `x-akr-token`), and only hashes of access tokens are kept while a box lives. Every box is AES-256-GCM encrypted between the user's devices and the requesting computer: the relay sees only random box IDs and ciphertext and can drop or delay a message, never read or forge one. A join, answer or update box is deleted as soon as it is picked up; unread boxes stop being served the moment their time runs out (10 minutes for a join or answer, 45 minutes for an approval grant that Stop marks, 7 days for a computer's update mailbox), and AWS then removes expired rows from DynamoDB automatically, usually within a few days. Computers join through the same relay with a one-time code that also encrypts the join. Stop on any device marks the approval's grant at the relay, and the computer checks the grant before every use. Each computer learns rule and device changes from its update mailbox, and uses Automatic passwords on its own only while it has heard from the user's devices in the last week. The Mac doesn't need to be awake; a computer can wake it with a push, if Agent Keyring is open (turn on Open at Login).
- Apple's push service sees notification metadata and the fallback text "A request is waiting." The website, account and reason are encrypted.
- The Apple Watch keeps its own copy of each password, encrypted so only that Apple Watch can open it, and sent to it by the iPhone directly. Copies the Mac encrypts for it pass through the user's own iCloud as that ciphertext. None goes to a computer or the relay. A computer allowed to use an Automatic password keeps a copy it can open itself.
- What the user is shown: the website, the account and the computer come from Agent Keyring and are signed, so an agent can't fake them. The agent's name and reason are the agent's own words.
- Rules and the list of devices are signed. Changing a rule or adding a device requires the user's approval, so an agent can't do either.
- Two-factor codes: Agent Keyring fills the codes that Apple Passwords generates for a site. For an Ask password, the agent's computer gets time-limited codes for those 30 minutes, and the setup key stays on the user's devices. For an Automatic password, an allowed computer can generate codes itself.
- After a denial, that computer can't ask for the same password again for 1 minute. After a second denial in a row it waits 5 minutes, then 15.
- Anonymous update check: once a day, Agent Keyring checks `https://push.opentrawl.sh/v1/version` with one stable, anonymous, non-reversible SHA-256 hash (derived from the app-scoped iCloud user ID when signed in, or a random local ID otherwise), app version, OS and CPU architecture (no IP addresses, Apple IDs or personal data stored). Users can opt out in Devices (Mac), Settings (iPhone), via `no_telemetry`, or by setting `AGENT_KEYRING_NO_TELEMETRY=1`.

## How it compares

Checked November 2026:

- **Agent Keyring:** Apple Passwords; free and open source (MIT); works with Claude Code, Codex and any agent that runs shell commands; approve on Mac (Touch ID), iPhone (Face ID) or Apple Watch (tap); one approval covers one password for one task, 30 minutes at most.
- **1Password for Agents:** 1Password; requires an individual or family account on 1Password.com; five partner apps (Claude Duet, Grok Bot, Instinct, Muse and Town), not Claude Code or Codex; approve in the 1Password app on the device the agent runs on; one approval covers one login for up to 30 days.
- **Bitwarden Agent Access:** Bitwarden; free and open source; works with any agent that runs shell commands; approve in an open terminal; one approval covers one request, or repeat requests from the same device for a chosen window.
- **Proton Pass CLI:** Proton Pass; free account or paid plan; works with any agent that runs shell commands; no per-request approval, session unlocks the vault until logout or timeout.

# Agent Keyring: Passwords for the Agentic OS

Published: 2026-11-20
Updated: 2026-11-24
Status: signed Mac app available on GitHub Releases (works with Touch ID); v1.1 needs no Tailscale and lets the iPhone work on its own; iPhone and Apple Watch public beta open on TestFlight at https://testflight.apple.com/join/W5xBNeMw
Made by: Josh Palmer (https://x.com/jjpcodes)
Website: https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/
Download (Mac): https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest
Source code: https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring
Licence: MIT (free)
Security: /security.md (https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/security.md)
Comparison: /compare.md (https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/compare.md)
Privacy: /privacy.md (https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/privacy.md)
Full context: /llms-full.txt (https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/llms-full.txt)

Your agents ask. You tap yes.

Passwords for the Agentic OS, part of the OpenTrawl suite (https://github.com/opentrawl). Let Claude Code, Codex or any AI agent sign in to websites with the passwords you keep in Apple Passwords, approved with Touch ID, Face ID or your Apple Watch.

## The walkthrough

The home page plays four short scenes.

1. Apple Watch. You're out on your bike. Claude Code, on the Mac mini at home, needs to sign in to openai.com to top up API credits. Your Apple Watch shows the website, the account and the reason. You tap Approve, and Claude Code signs in and carries on.
2. Mac. You're at your desk. Codex needs a password and a two-factor code for hetzner.com to download last month's invoices. You click Approve and use Touch ID. One approval covers both.
3. iPhone. You're on the toilet. Claude Code, on a Linux server, asks for your github.com password to make a new access token. You deny it and say "No. Use the gh CLI." Claude Code gets your reply and uses gh instead.
4. Without Agent Keyring. The same top-up task stalls for more than two hours, until you get home and sign in yourself.

## Set it up

There are two installs. The app goes on your own Mac with Touch ID, your iPhone and your Apple Watch: it holds your passwords and asks you to approve. Every Mac and iPhone is an equal: import from Apple Passwords on any of them and their lists merge through your own iCloud. No Mac? The iPhone app works on its own. The `agent-keyring` command goes on the computers your agents run on, such as a headless Mac mini, a Linux server or a cloud VM: it asks for passwords and holds no vault. Don't install the app on a computer that agents control.

On your own Mac, paste one prompt into Claude Code or Codex. Your agent downloads the Mac app, tells you what it suggests next, and asks before touching anything:

> Install and set up Agent Keyring using https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/llms.txt. Tell me what you plan to do and ask before changing anything.

1. Paste the prompt (or download the Mac app). Paste the prompt above into Claude Code or Codex, or download the signed Mac app yourself from GitHub Releases (https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest) (macOS 26 or later). Your agent verifies the checksum, installs it in `/Applications`, and asks before changing anything else.
2. Copy your passwords from Apple Passwords. In Apple Passwords, choose File > Export All Items to App… and pick Agent Keyring. Nothing is deleted from Passwords, and every password starts on Ask so no agent gets one until you approve.
3. Let your agent wire up the rest (with your say-so). Your agent reads `agent-keyring skill`, tells you what it recommends, and asks before touching your Chrome-family browser extension, enrolling Linux or Mac servers, or connecting your iPhone and Apple Watch (join the TestFlight beta at https://testflight.apple.com/join/W5xBNeMw or build from source).

With only an iPhone: open the app, tap Set Up on This iPhone, then in Apple Passwords tap Export Data to Another App and choose Agent Keyring. Add your Apple Watch and your agent computers from the iPhone's Devices tab.

## Each password has a rule

Every password starts on Ask. Change the rule whenever you like.

- Ask: an agent has to ask, and you approve or deny. One approval covers that one password for that one task, 30 minutes at most.
- Automatic: agents on the computers you choose get it without asking. Use it for a password you'd leave on that computer anyway, like the one for a staging site.
- Blocked: once a computer receives the rule, it refuses every request. Good for your bank and your email.

## How it works

Your agent runs a command, `agent-keyring`, and asks for one password by website. You see the website, the account, which agent on which computer is asking, and its reason. Approve, and Agent Keyring signs in for that task. There's no account and no vault of ours: your passwords stay encrypted on your own devices, and your Apple devices keep each other up to date through your own iCloud. We can't read your passwords, Apple can't read them, and your internet provider can't read them.

When an agent on another computer asks for approval, requests and answers pass through our zero-data-retention relay at `push.opentrawl.sh`: zero per-request logs, no box IDs or tokens in URLs, and AES-256-GCM encrypted boxes deleted the moment they're picked up. You can also self-host it with `agent-keyring-box`.

The computer your agent runs on (a Mac or a Linux server) sends the website, the account and the agent's reason to your devices (Mac, iPhone and Apple Watch). A Blocked password stops there. An approved request sends back one password, for one task, 30 minutes at most.

- Your passwords are encrypted on your own devices. Your Mac and iPhone encrypt their approval copies with keys kept in the Secure Enclave, the chip behind Touch ID and Face ID. Those keys can't leave the chip. A copy sent to another of your devices through iCloud is encrypted to that device's key first, so iCloud only ever holds ciphertext. A computer allowed to use an Automatic password keeps a copy it can open itself.
- Works in any browser, app or CLI. You just approve the request; your agent picks the right way to sign in. When it's in Chrome, Brave, Edge, Arc or Chromium with the extension loaded, the extension types the password straight into the form. In Safari, built-in agent browsers, desktop apps (via computer use) or CLI tools, your agent passes the approved password straight into the tool or app.
- One approval, one password, one task. An approval covers retries and ends when the agent releases it, when the computer receives your Stop, or after 30 minutes at most.
- Two-factor codes work too. If you set up a site's two-factor code in Apple Passwords, Agent Keyring fills it in along with the password. For an Ask password, your agent never gets the setup key, so it can't make codes of its own later.

Security details: /security.md

## Already use Apple Passwords?

Then you don't need a second password manager, a new account or a subscription. Checked November 2026:

| | Agent Keyring | 1Password for Agents | Bitwarden Agent Access |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where your passwords live | Apple Passwords | 1Password | Bitwarden |
| Cost | Free and open source (MIT) | An individual or family account on 1Password.com | Free and open source |
| Agents it works with | Claude Code, Codex and anything else that can run a shell command | Five partner apps. Not Claude Code or Codex | Anything that can run a shell command |
| Where you approve | Mac, iPhone or Apple Watch | The 1Password app, on the device the agent runs on | A terminal you keep open |
| What one approval covers | One password for one task, 30 minutes at most | One login, for up to 30 days | One request, or repeat requests from the same device for a time you choose |

Full comparison: /compare.md

## Questions

- Does my Mac have to stay awake? No. Your iPhone keeps its own encrypted copy of your passwords, and an agent on another computer sends its request straight to your iPhone and Apple Watch. That agent can sign in while your MacBook is shut in a bag.
- Can I use a Mac mini or Mac Studio without Touch ID? Yes, two ways. If agents run on it, install only the `agent-keyring` command and add it from your Mac or iPhone with a one-time code. If it is your own personal Mac, the app asks how you use it and you can opt in to approving with your Mac password. Your passwords stay locked to its Secure Enclave, and no agent can open an Ask password without macOS asking for your Mac password, but a typed password is weaker than Touch ID or Face ID: an agent or tool that knows your Mac login password could approve its own requests.
- How do my Mac and iPhone find each other? Through your own iCloud Keychain, which Apple encrypts end to end. After that they keep each other up to date through your own iCloud. There is no account with us.
- Do I need a Mac? No. The iPhone app can hold your passwords on its own: export from Apple Passwords on the iPhone, add your Apple Watch, and add agent computers with a one-time code.
- Do I need Tailscale? No. Agent computers join with a one-time code (`agent-keyring enrol --code`). Requests and answers pass through our zero-data-retention relay of AES-256-GCM encrypted boxes, which runs with zero per-request logs, keeps box IDs and access tokens out of URLs, deletes each box when it is picked up, stops serving unread boxes when their time runs out, and lets AWS remove expired rows from DynamoDB automatically (usually within a few days). You can run your own with `agent-keyring-box`.
- What does zero data retention mean on the relay? The relay Lambda at `push.opentrawl.sh` has zero `console.*` calls, no CloudWatch Logs permissions in its IAM role, and its CloudWatch log group is destroyed. Requests hit fixed endpoints (`/v1/box`, `/v1/push`) with random box IDs and access tokens sent only in headers (`x-akr-box`, `x-akr-token`), and only hashes of access tokens are kept while a box lives. Unread boxes stop being served at expiry (10 minutes for a join or answer, 45 minutes for an approval grant that Stop marks, 7 days for an update mailbox), after which AWS removes expired rows from DynamoDB automatically, usually within a few days. See /security.md for full details.
- Does it work in Safari, desktop apps, or the browsers built into Codex, Claude and T3 Code? Yes. You approve once, and your agent handles how to sign in: using the browser extension in Chrome-family browsers, or passing the approved password straight into Safari, built-in agent browsers, desktop apps via computer use, or CLI tools.
- What is the Chrome extension for? It lets your agent sign in to Chrome, Brave, Edge, Arc or Chromium without the password touching the agent's own tool output or chat. Your agent uses it automatically when it's available, and falls back to the CLI anywhere else.
- I saved a new password. Does Agent Keyring pick it up? Not by itself. Apple only hands passwords to another app when you start the export, so export again: File > Export All Items to App… on a Mac, or Export Data to Another App on an iPhone. Either one updates every device. You can turn on a reminder, off by default, that comes once your copy is a week old.
- What about passkeys and SMS codes? Neither. Agent Keyring handles passwords and the two-factor codes Apple Passwords generates. It can't use passkeys or read codes sent by SMS or email.

## Join the iPhone and Apple Watch beta

The signed Mac app is out on GitHub Releases (https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/releases/latest) and works straight away with Touch ID. The iPhone and Apple Watch apps are in public beta on TestFlight: open https://testflight.apple.com/join/W5xBNeMw on your iPhone to install them. Source code: https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring

# Agent Keyring security

Published: 2026-11-21
Updated: 2026-11-24
Made by: Josh Palmer (https://x.com/jjpcodes)

Threat model in the source: https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring/blob/main/docs/threat-model.md
Home: /index.md
Comparison: /compare.md
Privacy: /privacy.md

There's no account and no vault of ours. Your passwords stay encrypted on your own devices, our relay runs with zero data retention, and an agent gets a password only when you approve it or when you've set that password to Automatic.

## Where your passwords are

Your Mac, iPhone and Apple Watch each keep their own encrypted copies of your passwords, with keys in their Secure Enclave, the chip behind Touch ID and Face ID. Those keys can't leave the chip. Your iPhone sends your Apple Watch its copies directly. Copies your Mac encrypts for your Apple Watch pass through your own iCloud on the way, as ciphertext only your Apple Watch can open. No computer and no relay ever carries them.

A Mac without Touch ID, such as a Mac mini or Mac Studio, keeps your passwords only if you opt in to approving with its Mac password. Its keys are still in its Secure Enclave, and no agent can open an Ask password without macOS asking for that password. A typed password is weaker than Touch ID or Face ID: an agent or tool that knows your Mac login password, for example from a `sudo` prompt, could approve its own requests. If you add a Touch ID keyboard or an Apple Watch later, macOS accepts those too, and the password still works. A computer that only runs agents should have only the `agent-keyring` command, never the app.

Your Mac and iPhone find each other through your own iCloud Keychain, which Apple encrypts end to end.

## Keeping your devices in step

Every Mac and iPhone is an equal: none is in charge, and you can copy from Apple Passwords on any of them. They keep each other up to date through your own iCloud private database. Each password is encrypted to the receiving device's Secure Enclave key before it leaves the device you copied it on, so iCloud only ever holds ciphertext: we can't read your passwords, Apple can't, and your internet provider can't. The list of devices and the list of passwords and rules are signed by one of your devices, and every device checks those signatures, so nobody who can write to your iCloud can add a device or change a rule.

The list of websites and account names is kept in CloudKit's encrypted fields. With Advanced Data Protection on, only your devices can read it; without it, Apple holds the keys, as it does for the rest of your iCloud data. Each device's list of passwords is signed with that device's key too, and a rule only ever comes from a list you approved with Touch ID or Face ID.

If two devices change the same password's rule at once, the later change wins on every device. Blocking a password deletes it from every device.

## What your agent sees

You approve once, and your agent's skill picks the cleanest route for whatever it's driving. In Chrome, Brave, Edge, Arc or Chromium with the extension loaded, the agent names the form fields and the extension checks the website, types the password, submits and clears the fields so nothing enters chat or logs.

Anywhere the extension doesn't run (built-in agent browsers, Safari, desktop apps via computer use, or command-line tools such as `gh`), the agent passes the approved password straight into the code, app or tool through `agent-keyring read`, which refuses to print to a terminal.

## How push notifications work

Agents on your Mac ask the Mac app directly, with no network hop at all. When an agent on another computer needs your iPhone, Apple Watch or Mac, it encrypts the request (website, account and reason) for your devices and sends that opaque payload through our stateless blind push relay at `push.opentrawl.sh` (AWS `eu-west-1`). The relay signs the request with our Apple Developer push key and forwards it to Apple's push servers, without storing raw device tokens, IP addresses or message contents. Apple sees only standard notification metadata and the fallback text "A request is waiting."

Your approval answer is encrypted for the one computer that asked and waits for it in an ephemeral box at `push.opentrawl.sh`. Computers join the same way, with a one-time code that also encrypts their join request so the relay can't read or change it. Stop on any of your devices marks the approval stopped at the relay, and the computer checks there before every use, so an approval it can't check isn't used. macOS doesn't open a quit app for a push, so turn on Open Agent Keyring at Login if you want your Mac to answer agents on other computers.

## Zero data retention on our relay

The relay at `push.opentrawl.sh` (AWS `eu-west-1`) is built for zero data retention:

- **Zero per-request logs:** the relay Lambda has zero `console.*` calls, its IAM role has no CloudWatch Logs permissions, and the `/aws/lambda/opentrawl-push-relay` CloudWatch log group is destroyed.
- **No box IDs or tokens in URLs:** clients talk to fixed endpoints (`/v1/box`, `/v1/push`) with random box IDs and access tokens sent only in headers (`x-akr-box`, `x-akr-token`), and only hashes of access tokens are kept while a box lives.
- **End-to-end encrypted boxes:** every box is AES-256-GCM encrypted between your devices and the requesting computer. The relay sees only random box IDs and ciphertext: it can drop or delay a message, never read or forge one.
- **Deletion and expiry:** a join, answer or update box is deleted as soon as it is picked up. Unread boxes stop being served the moment their time runs out (10 minutes for a join or answer, 45 minutes for an approval grant that Stop marks, 7 days for a computer's update mailbox), and AWS then removes expired rows from DynamoDB automatically, usually within a few days.

You can self-host the relay with `agent-keyring-box` behind HTTPS with a certificate your iPhone and Apple Watch trust, such as one from Let's Encrypt. If you build the apps with your own Apple Developer account, you can run your own push relay or push straight to Apple instead.

## Anonymous update check

Once a day, Agent Keyring checks `https://push.opentrawl.sh/v1/version` with one stable, anonymous, non-reversible SHA-256 hash (derived from your app-scoped iCloud user ID when signed in, or a random local ID otherwise), app version, OS and CPU architecture so it can notify you of new releases and let us count active users. No IP addresses, Apple IDs, websites, accounts or passwords are sent or stored. Those daily and monthly counts expire after 90 days. Push counts are kept apart from them: to limit abuse and count daily pushes, the relay keeps SHA-256 hashes of device tokens, for 1 hour and 35 days. You can turn it off in Devices (Mac), Settings (iPhone), via `no_telemetry`, or with `AGENT_KEYRING_NO_TELEMETRY=1`. See the privacy policy at /privacy.md (https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/privacy/) for full details.

## What you're shown

Every request shows the website, the account and the computer that asked. Agent Keyring fills those in itself, so an agent can't fake them. The agent's name and its reason are the agent's own words, which is why the reason sits in quotation marks. An agent tricked by a web page can write anything there.

Changing a rule or adding a device requires your approval, so an agent can't switch a password to Automatic or add a computer of its own.

## What an approval covers

One password, for one task, for 30 minutes at most. Retries and the two-factor step are included. Access ends when the agent releases it, when the computer receives your Stop, or after 30 minutes. For an Ask password, the agent's computer gets time-limited codes for those 30 minutes, and the setup key stays on your devices.

If you deny a request, that computer waits a minute before it can ask for the same password again. Deny it twice in a row and it waits five minutes, then fifteen.

## Automatic passwords

A computer you choose keeps its own encrypted copy of each Automatic password, two-factor setup key included, so agents there can sign in while you sleep. Only use Automatic for a password you'd leave on that computer anyway. Switch it back to Ask and a computer deletes its copy when it receives the updated list from your Mac or iPhone. It receives that list from its update mailbox, which your Mac and iPhone write after every change and once a day, or with the next answer to one of its requests. A computer that hasn't heard from your devices for a week stops using its Automatic passwords on its own.

## What each device keeps

| Device | What it keeps | What it can open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your Mac | An encrypted copy of every password you copied from Apple Passwords | One password per approval, after Touch ID (or your Mac password, on a Mac without Touch ID that you opted in) |
| Your iPhone | Its own encrypted copy of your passwords | One password per approval, after Face ID |
| Your iCloud private database | The signed lists, each device's list of passwords without the passwords, and copies encrypted to each device | Nothing: every copy opens only on the device it was encrypted for |
| Your Apple Watch | Its own encrypted copy of every password that isn't Blocked | One password per approval, when you tap Approve on your wrist |
| A computer your agents run on | The website and account name of each password, and its own encrypted copy of each Automatic password | Its Automatic passwords, and an Ask password once you approve it |
| Our zero-data-retention relay (`push.opentrawl.sh`) | Zero per-request logs. Only AES-256-GCM ciphertext boxes under random IDs and hashed access tokens until picked up or expired | Nothing: it can drop or delay a message, never read or forge one |

## What it can't do

- Watch what an agent does once it's signed in. Ending an approval doesn't sign the agent out of the website either.
- Take a password back. Stop and the 30-minute limit end what Agent Keyring hands out. They don't erase what a computer already received.
- Stop an agent that goes looking for the password. While the extension fills a form (its normal wait is up to 20 seconds before clearing the fields), an agent that controls that browser can read the password there. An agent can also pipe a password into a program it wrote itself.
- Protect an unlocked Mac. Someone sitting at it can ask for passwords like any agent there. They still need your approval for an Ask password, but not for an Automatic one.
- Wipe a lost iPhone. Remove it in Devices and it gets no more requests, but its copy of your passwords stays on the phone behind Face ID. If someone may get past that, change those passwords.
- Keep passwords out of the agent outside the browser extension. In built-in browsers, Safari, computer use or CLI tools, the agent handles the password itself via `agent-keyring read`.
- Use passkeys or codes sent by SMS or email.
- Sync with Apple Passwords. Apple only hands passwords over when you start an export, so export again after you change one, on your Mac or iPhone. A reminder, off by default, can tell you once your copy is a week old.
- Hide which websites you have from Apple without Advanced Data Protection. Your passwords stay sealed either way.

# How Agent Keyring compares

Published: 2026-11-20
Updated: 2026-11-24
Made by: Josh Palmer (https://x.com/jjpcodes)
HTML page: https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/compare/
Home: /index.md
Security: /security.md
Source code: https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring

1Password, Bitwarden and Proton Pass can each hand a password to an agent, as long as your passwords are in their app. Agent Keyring uses the ones you already keep in Apple Passwords, and you approve on your Mac, iPhone or Apple Watch.

## Which is better: Agent Keyring, 1Password for Agents, Bitwarden or Proton Pass?

It depends on where your passwords live and which agents you run. As of November 2026, choose Agent Keyring if you use Apple Passwords on a Mac and run Claude Code, Codex or shell-based agents with Touch ID, Face ID or Apple Watch approvals. Choose 1Password for Agents if your vault is in 1Password and you use one of its five partner apps; Bitwarden Agent Access if you use Bitwarden or approve on Linux, Windows or Android; Proton Pass access tokens for unattended vault access.

## Side by side

Checked on 22 November 2026 against the 1Password (https://support.1password.com/1password-for-agents/), Bitwarden (https://github.com/bitwarden/agent-access) and Proton Pass (https://proton.me/support/pass-access-tokens) documentation.

| | Agent Keyring | 1Password for Agents | Bitwarden Agent Access | Proton Pass access tokens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where your passwords live | Apple Passwords. You copy them to your Mac, and again when one changes | 1Password | Bitwarden. The protocol is open to other password managers | Proton Pass |
| Cost | Free and open source (MIT) | An individual or family account on 1Password.com | Free and open source | A Proton plan that includes Pass access tokens |
| Agents it works with | Claude Code, Codex and anything else that can run a shell command | Five partner apps: Claude Duet, Grok Bot, Instinct, Muse and Town | Anything that can run a shell command | Anything that can run the Proton Pass command-line tool |
| Where you approve | Mac (Touch ID), iPhone (Face ID) or Apple Watch (one tap) | The 1Password app, on the device the agent runs on | The terminal running `aac listen` | Nowhere. You choose vaults when you make the token |
| What one approval covers | One password for one task, 30 minutes at most | One login, for up to 30 days | One request, or repeat requests from the same device for a time you choose | Every item in the vaults you chose, for 1 hour to 1 year |
| Can the agent read the password? | Not in chat when the agent fills via the browser extension (an agent controlling that browser can still read the filled field). Yes when the agent falls back to the CLI for other browsers, computer use or CLI tools | No. 1Password fills it outside the agent's view | Yes, unless it uses `aac run`, which passes it to a program instead | Yes |
| What you can answer | Approve, deny, or deny and tell the agent what to do instead, typed or spoken | Approve, pick a different login, or deny | Approve once, approve repeats for a time you choose, or deny | Nothing to answer |
| Agents on a Linux server | Yes, with a one-time code; no Tailscale needed | Only where the 1Password app and a partner app both run | Yes, through a relay that can't read the traffic | Yes |

## Choose Agent Keyring if

Your passwords are in Apple Passwords, you work on a Mac, and your agents are Claude Code, Codex or anything else that runs shell commands, on that Mac or on a Linux server.

## Choose something else if

Your passwords already live in 1Password, Bitwarden or Proton Pass, you need shared team vaults, or you want to approve from Android or Windows.

# Agent Keyring privacy policy

Updated: 2026-11-24
Website: https://keyring.opentrawl.sh/privacy/
Source code: https://github.com/opentrawl/agent-keyring

Agent Keyring keeps your passwords on your own devices. There is no account, no vault of ours, and no ad or tracking SDK.

## Passwords and approvals

Your passwords stay encrypted on your own Mac, iPhone and Apple Watch, protected by keys kept in each device's Secure Enclave. They are never uploaded to any OpenTrawl or Agent Keyring server. Your Macs and iPhones keep each other up to date through your own iCloud private database, which we have no access to; every password there is encrypted to the receiving device's Secure Enclave key first. An approval may also carry that computer's own copies of its Automatic passwords, each encrypted so only that computer can open it.

## Zero-data-retention encrypted relay

When you pair a computer, answer an approval request, send a Stop signal or deliver a rule update, the message travels through our zero-data-retention relay at `push.opentrawl.sh` (AWS `eu-west-1`, Ireland), or your own self-hosted `agent-keyring-box`:

- **Zero per-request logs:** the relay Lambda has zero `console.*` calls, its IAM role has no CloudWatch Logs permissions, and the `/aws/lambda/opentrawl-push-relay` CloudWatch log group is destroyed.
- **No box IDs or tokens in URLs:** fixed endpoints (`/v1/box`, `/v1/push`) take random box IDs and access tokens only in headers (`x-akr-box`, `x-akr-token`), and only hashes of access tokens are kept while a box lives.
- **End-to-end encrypted boxes:** every box is AES-256-GCM encrypted between your devices and the requesting computer. The relay sees only random box IDs and ciphertext and can drop or delay a message, never read or forge one.
- **Deletion and expiry:** a join, answer or update box is deleted as soon as it is picked up. Unread boxes stop being served the moment their time runs out (10 minutes for a join or answer, 45 minutes for an approval grant that Stop marks, 7 days for a computer's update mailbox), and AWS then removes expired rows from DynamoDB automatically, usually within a few days.

## Blind push notification relay

When an agent on another computer asks your iPhone or Apple Watch to approve a sign-in, it sends an end-to-end encrypted push payload through our stateless push relay at `push.opentrawl.sh` (hosted on AWS in `eu-west-1`, Ireland). The relay signs the request with our Apple Developer push key and forwards the opaque payload straight to Apple's push servers.

The relay cannot read the website, account name or reason inside the payload. It stores no raw device tokens, no IP addresses and no message contents. To prevent abuse and count daily push volume, it keeps only short-lived SHA-256 hashes of device tokens (1 hour for rate limiting, 35 days for daily counts). If you build the apps with your own Apple Developer account, you can run your own relay or push straight to Apple instead.

## Anonymous update check

Once a day, Agent Keyring checks `https://push.opentrawl.sh/v1/version` to see if a newer release is available and to count active users. That check sends one stable, anonymous, non-reversible SHA-256 hash (derived from your app-scoped iCloud user identifier when signed in so your Mac and iPhone count as one user, or a random local identifier otherwise), the app version, the operating system (`macos`, `ios`, `watchos` or `linux`) and CPU architecture. It never sends passwords, website names, account names, Apple IDs or personal details, and the server does not store IP addresses. Daily and monthly counts expire automatically after 90 days.

You can turn the update check off at any time in **Devices** (Mac) or **Settings** (iPhone), via the `no_telemetry` preference, or by setting `AGENT_KEYRING_NO_TELEMETRY=1`.

## Beta waitlist emails

If you submit your email address and device checkboxes on `keyring.opentrawl.sh`, we store them in AWS (`eu-west-1`) solely to send you Agent Keyring beta and TestFlight invites. We do not sell, rent or share your email address with anyone.

## Contact

To delete your waitlist email or ask about privacy, email josh@jjpcodes.com or message @jjpcodes (https://x.com/jjpcodes).
